sūcīhasta
(‘needle [pose] of hand’)
------------------------------------------
This is one of the hand-poses shown in the images of gods and goddesses. It is a gesture of the right hand, in which the forefinger is held upright and all the other fingers are pressed against the palm. It signifies several things such as threat, warning, beating of drum, truth, or the numbers one and hundred.
The pose is also called sūcīmukhahasta.

Śucīndram
(‘[the place where] इन्द्र was purified’)
------------------------------------------
Śucīndram is mainly famous for its beautiful temple built in the 17th century. It is 13 kms. (8 miles) from the famous पिल्ग्रिमगे centre, कन्याकुमारी, the southern-most tip of the Indian peninsula.
शुचीन्द्रम् Temple">A View of the शुचीन्द्रम् TempleThe main shrine is contained in the hollow of a laurel tree, believed to be 2000 years old. It is one लिङ्ग representing all the three Hindu deities, ब्रह्मा, विष्णु and शिव. The bottom of the लिङ्ग represents ब्रह्मा, the middle part विष्णु and the top शिव.
The sage couple, अत्रि and अनसूया, got a boon that the three deities should be born as their children. Consequently they took birth as चन्द्र, दत्तात्रेय and दुर्वासस्. This लिङ्ग is the combined form of these three.
The entrance gopuram (main gate) is a seven-storeyed structure 40 metres (134 ft.) high. There is a huge carved नन्दि (Śiva’s bull) said to be 800 years old. At the entrance to the main temple are two large door-keepers.
According to the local legend, इन्द्र who had committed the sin of अदुल्तेर्य् with अहल्या, did तपस् (severe austerity) here, worshipping the Trimūrtis (the three deities mentioned above), and was purified. The very name शुचीन्द्रम् (śuci = purification; of इन्द्र) indicates this.
The temple campus contains 30 minor shrines dedicated to विष्णु (with a metallic image of eight metals), Sītārāma, गणेश and नवग्रहस् (the nine प्लनेत्स्). There is also an image of हनुमान् 5.4 metres (18 ft.) high.
Sculptures from the Rāmāyaṇa and the Mahābhārata as also the four musical pillars of stone carved out of a single block of granite are added attractions. Each pillar gives the sound of a different instrument, that of mṛdaṅga, sitār, tampūra and jalataraṅga.
On Fridays there is a special sun-set ceremony. Daily rituals, however, close before dusk since इन्द्र is believed to come then and perform the worship, the whole night.
Non-Hindus are allowed to enter this temple.
